question: How is the command to read introduced in the sentence?

positions.position: An omitted saying introduces direct speech to the person.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī compare omitted speech in 40:46 and 3:106. Al-Ṭabarī identifies God as speaker and the angels' deed-register as object; al-Rāzī says God speaks through angels. Al-Samīn allows the clause to be adjectival or circumstantial; al-Ālūsī also allows an independent sentence. Ibn ʿĀshūr says context makes the speaker plain.

question: How is the imperative ٱقْرَأْ formed or pronounced?

positions.position: Its imperative drops the hamza's ḍamma; a light or replaced hamza is also reported.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās adduces Arab replacement of hamza and Zuhayr's line وإلا يبد بالظلم يظلم; Ibn al-Jawzī reports Abū Jaʿfar's light hamza.

question: Can someone who was unable to read in life read the record then?

positions.position: Yes; everyone reads the record at resurrection, including the formerly illiterate.
positions.reasons: Qatāda is repeatedly transmitted; al-Ḥasan says literate and illiterate alike. Al-Biqāʿī says God grants the ability and each reads personally. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows miraculous understanding of inscriptions.

question: What does reading one's book mean here?

positions.position: The person reads or understands the displayed account of deeds.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī calls it the angels' counted register; Ibn ʿĀshūr says reading can mean knowledge of recorded deeds or miraculous understanding of writing. Al-Biqāʿī stresses personal reading rather than another reader. Al-Ṭabrisī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī report that the person recalls every deed as if performing it then, explaining 18:49.

positions.position: The intellect reads the soul's exposed impressions when bodily attachment ends.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī says each deed leaves a lasting effect, like water drops boring stone; conventional letters signify sounds by agreement, whereas soul impressions are intrinsic. He cites 50:22 and affirms outward reports as true too. Al-Ālūsī calls this remote from the plain sense; Asad reports al-Rāzī's allegory of complete recollection.

turns_on: Whether reading concerns a displayed register or the soul's disclosed knowledge.

question: Why command the person to read the record?

positions.position: It establishes proof by making the person recognize and confess the deeds, leaving no excuse.
positions.reasons: Al-Māwardī says reading makes one acknowledge the deeds. Al-Jishumī says it completes proof and shows no injustice. Al-Ṭabrisī says every deed and recompense is seen. Ibn al-Jawzī adds that Hell follows sin while Paradise is grace. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a compelled challenge and says the person already knows the deeds.

positions.position: It heightens reproach and rebuke.
positions.reasons: Al-Māwardī offers this as another purpose of making the person read.

turns_on: Whether the imperative primarily elicits acknowledgment or sharpens rebuke.

question: What is the person's book?

positions.position: It is the complete record of the person's deeds, displayed at resurrection.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī says recording angels keep and count it; al-Ḥasan's report says two noble angels write it, roll it at death, and place it around the neck until resurrection. Study Quran cites 82:10–12 and lists parallels 17:71, 18:49, 69:19, 69:25, 84:7, 84:10. Al-Biqāʿī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī say no deed is omitted; the latter says it was already prepared but is brought out from heedlessness.

positions.position: The book is the actual deeds and their revealed realities, rather than ordinary written signs.
positions.reasons: Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 3:30 and 50:22: deeds themselves appear with consequences, and the clinging 'bird' and book name the same deed. Their exposure confirms unavoidable recompense and removes concealment.

positions.position: The book can be the soul inscribed with enduring traces of deeds.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī likens habitual acts to drops wearing stone; soul impressions outlast conventional letters and become apparent on separation from the body. Study Quran reports this and cites bodily testimony at 24:24, 36:65, 41:20–22. Al-Ālūsī calls the reading remote but reports the view that outward and inward senses coexist. Al-Rāzī says the impressions reveal felicity or misery and explicitly affirms this spiritual sense alongside outward narrated events.

positions.position: The book can represent the person and full recollection of the past life.
positions.reasons: Some commentators in Study Quran picture tongue as pen, saliva as ink, limbs as page and memory as dictated record; al-Qurṭubī gives tongue, saliva and limbs as a pious saying. Asad transmits al-Rāzī's allegory of complete comprehension, citing 37:19, 39:68 and 50:22.

turns_on: Whether 'book' denotes the written register, deeds themselves, or a figurative record within the person.

question: What does a report say happens when a believer receives and reads the book?

positions.position: A believer sees sins within and good deeds outside, then learns the sins were forgiven and rejoices.
positions.reasons: Ubayy says the person led many to good, fears sins, finds them forgiven and good deeds doubled; his face brightens, he receives the book in his right hand, a crown, two garments, ornaments at every joint and Adam's sixty-cubit stature, then announces the reward to companions with 69:19–23. Bakr says the visible good deeds draw envy, and private forgiveness brings joy, citing 69:19 and, in al-Rāzī, 80:38–39. Al-Ālūsī's version begins with feared sins, then forgiven sins and increasing light and joy, citing 69:19–20.

question: What does a report say happens when an unbeliever reads the book?

positions.position: The unbeliever sees good deeds rejected and then sins, with darkness and lament.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī's report cites 25:23 for rejected deeds and 69:25–26 for the lament.

question: What is the grammatical subject of كَفَىٰ and the function of ب in بِنَفْسِكَ?

positions.position: Nafsika is the subject in nominative position; bāʾ is added for emphasis.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ says the bāʾ can be omitted with a raised noun in praise or blame, unlike ordinary verbs, and adduces كفى الهدي. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī cite poetry without bāʾ; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 4:79. Al-Ālūsī calls this the majority parse.

positions.position: The subject is an implicit notion of sufficiency, so bāʾ is not extra.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn mention this analysis; al-Ālūsī includes it among alternatives. Al-Burhān supplies kāna after kafā, with bi-nafsika its predicate, or a pronoun explained by accusative ḥasīban as in نعم رجلا زيد.

positions.position: Kafā is an imperative-like form with an implicit addressee, and bāʾ is not extra.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn finds the analysis weak because kafā accepts verbal inflections; al-Ālūsī says the majority prefers the ordinary past-verb parse. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the indeclinable imperative-like meaning اكتف.

turns_on: Whether the bāʾ introduces the overt subject or belongs to a different analysis of kafā.

question: Why is كَفَىٰ masculine although نَفْسِكَ is grammatically feminine?

positions.position: Masculine agreement is permitted because nafs is grammatically, not naturally, feminine.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn cites Qur'anic feminine agreement at 21:6 and 6:4 yet allows masculine for figurative gender; Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes the same point. Al-Ālūsī notes the difficulty and analogous verbs that do agree in feminine.

positions.position: The lack of feminine agreement argues that bāʾ is not extra and nafs is not the subject.
positions.reasons: Al-Burhān reasons that if bāʾ were extra, kafā would agree with normally feminine nafs; he offers omitted kāna or an explanatory pronoun as parses.

turns_on: Whether masculine agreement is allowed with the feminine noun nafs.

question: What does بِنَفْسِكَ refer to as the sufficient witness?

positions.position: It means the person's own self and knowledge of the deeds.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān calls this the apparent sense and notes Abū ʿUbayda's emphasis on what the person knows; Ibn Kathīr says the person remembers and knows no injustice or alien deed was recorded. Al-Ālūsī calls the bodily-limbs reading contrary to the apparent meaning.

positions.position: It means the person's bodily limbs testifying if the person denies.
positions.reasons: Muqātil compares the denial in 6:23 and testimony in 75:14, specifying self, tongue, hands and feet. Al-Biqāʿī says the tongue may deny but limbs confirm the precise record. Abū Ḥayyān transmits Muqātil; al-Ālūsī objects that this departs from the apparent meaning.

turns_on: Whether self-witnessing is the person's direct knowledge or testimony of bodily members.

question: What does ٱلْيَوْمَ modify?

positions.position: It is the time adverb governed by kafā.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn gives the attachment; al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī call it the adverb.

question: What does حَسِيبًا mean?

positions.position: An accountant or reckoner who audits and calls to account.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba gives the active sense beside sufficient; al-Wāḥidī compares God's epithet in 33:39. Al-Zamakhsharī likens the form to occupational nouns; al-Kalbī and others give accountant or intensive reckoner. Al-Qurṭubī's pious saying pictures tongue as pen, saliva as ink and limbs as witnesses.

positions.position: A witness against oneself.
positions.reasons: Muqātil says no better witness than oneself can be found; al-Zajjāj says the self suffices as witness. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī explain that a witness suffices a claimant in the matter at issue.

positions.position: One who suffices, standing in place of a witness or accountant.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba offers sufficient as an alternative to reckoner; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī say the witness suffices the claimant. Al-Zajjāj allows non-Qur'anic feminine ḥasība.

turns_on: Whether ḥasīb is understood from counting and judgment or from sufficiency and testimony.

question: What is the syntactic role of حَسِيبًا?

positions.position: It is an accusative specification, clarifying how the self suffices.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj states tamyīz. Al-Naḥḥās, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī also mention a circumstantial alternative; al-Sarrāj specifically posits an omitted subject for that parse.

positions.position: It is a circumstantial accusative.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās allows ḥāl as well as specification; al-Ṭabrisī attributes this with an omitted subject to al-Sarrāj. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī report it too.

turns_on: Whether the accusative specifies the sufficiency or describes the person's state.

question: Why is حَسِيبًا masculine with feminine نَفْس?

positions.position: Nafs means a person, so the description follows the person's sense.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī and others also point to male-associated roles such as witness, judge and trustee; al-Samīn cites a poem. Al-Bursawī takes nafs as person; al-Ālūsī also mentions the adjective pattern. Abū Isḥāq permits feminine ḥasība outside Qur'anic wording.

positions.position: Nafs lacks a visible feminine marker, allowing masculine description.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Anbārī compares sky and earth, citing 73:18; Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān cite poetry with masculine description of earth, including أبقل.

turns_on: Whether agreement follows the referent's sense or the noun's formal shape.

question: How does عَلَيْكَ connect syntactically and semantically?

positions.position: It depends on the sense of ḥasīb as one who reckons against a person.
positions.reasons: Al-Nasafī cites the idiom 'reckoned this against him'; al-Samīn cites al-Zamakhsharī and examples from Sībawayh; al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī agree. Ibn ʿĀshūr says ʿalayka implies testimony against the person.

positions.position: It marks the matter about which a sufficient witness answers the claimant.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī and al-Samīn give the witness construction as an alternative.

turns_on: Whether ḥasīb is construed as an accountant or a sufficient witness.

question: What does it mean that the person suffices as their own reckoner?

positions.position: One's own knowledge, record and confession suffice to account for and judge one's deeds, proving the judgment fair.
positions.reasons: Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī say no outside witness or recorder is needed; al-Ḥasan repeatedly calls this justice. Al-Jishumī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Bursawī say it removes excuses and establishes proof. Ibn Kathīr says the person remembers the deeds and no alien deed appears; Ibn al-Jawzī contrasts Paradise by grace and Hell by sin. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 66:7 for unavoidable evidence.

positions.position: The person's own limbs testify when the tongue denies the deeds.
positions.reasons: Muqātil illustrates this through 6:23 and 75:14; al-Biqāʿī says the record omits nothing and limbs answer denial.

turns_on: Whether the sufficient self-testimony is direct self-accounting or bodily testimony.

question: Who is addressed by the command?

positions.position: Every person, believer and unbeliever, faces the command and account.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī explicitly rejects restricting it to unbelievers merely because al-Suddī tells an unbeliever's story. Ibn ʿĀshūr points back to the person in 17:13; the believer and unbeliever reports cover both.

positions.position: In al-Suddī's reported episode, an unbeliever asks to audit himself and is told to read.
positions.reasons: The unbeliever invokes God's declaration that He is not unjust to servants. Al-Ālūsī says this episode does not limit the verse's general address.

turns_on: Whether a specific report about an unbeliever limits the general address.

question: What afterlife events does this verse establish?

positions.position: There will be a record, resurrection, precise reckoning and just recompense for one's own deeds.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī explicitly names afterlife reckoning and records. Al-Ṭabarī says angels keep the register; Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses exhaustive knowledge. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says deeds cling to their doer and their consequences inevitably appear. Iṣlāḥī says nobody bears another's burden; Kuranyolu says each sees the result; Study Quran cites 3:117, 10:44 and 29:40 for people wronging themselves.

question: What does the command imply about who creates the act of reading?

positions.position: The command would lose its function if God created the person's act of reading.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī uses the imperative itself against the doctrine that God creates the commanded act.

question: What does self-accounting imply for responsibility and divine justice?

positions.position: People are accountable for their deeds; reckoning proves God does not wrong them.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī argues that determinism would make God accountable for the deed, and that creating disbelief while preventing faith would make accounting pointless and unjust. Al-Bursawī says the person's own confession establishes proof. Study Quran says actions lead to salvation or condemnation, while mercy remains beyond calculation.

question: How should people prepare now for this self-accounting?

positions.position: Audit and weigh one's deeds before the final presentation while amendment is possible.
positions.reasons: ʿUmar's repeated counsel adds preparing for the great presentation; al-Bursawī stresses that tomorrow offers no repair. Al-Ḥasan urges a sound answer to questioning or a shroud for the Fire. Al-Sulamī contrasts righteous people reckoned now with wicked people reckoned later. Elmalılı urges daily examination. A Kashf al-Asrār report's king makes his self recount each evening's words, deeds, movements and stillness, which it finds hard to bear even for one day.

positions.position: In choosing among worthy acts, perform the one nearer to and weightier with God first.
positions.reasons: Sahl's context concerns duties, sunnas and voluntary acts; Tustarī presents this as practical self-accounting.

turns_on: Whether the practical counsel concerns reviewing deeds or prioritizing current acts.

question: Where does self-accounting take place?

positions.position: It may be private between servant and God or public between the person and others.
positions.reasons: Sahl gives both spheres as forms of self-accounting.

question: Why can a person be said to have authored their book?

positions.position: The person's own acts dictated its contents.
positions.reasons: Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh says people should read the book because they themselves dictated it; Study Quran's reported image makes memory dictate the record while tongue, saliva and limbs form its writing implements.

question: How does this account connect with the preceding passage?

positions.position: Revelation and warning have supplied proof, leaving no excuse when records are judged.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī says the completed account of signs and warning leads to the record; al-Ālūsī relays his proof of oneness, prophethood and resurrection. Kuranyolu likewise connects revelation, faith, reward and punishment to responsibility.

positions.position: God's worldly and religious benefits call for obedience, which is then examined.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī give this as a second link.

positions.position: Creation is for worship, and the sun, moon, night and day aid obedience that judgment assesses.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī cite 51:56; the latter says judgment asks whether people obeyed or rebelled.

positions.position: The passage moves from God's guidance-book to the person's exhaustive deed-book.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī cites 18:49: the personal book shows whether the first book was followed.

positions.position: The precise personal record makes the preceding general declaration of God's knowledge concrete.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr links encouragement and warning to 17:9–12, saying specific human deeds follow the general 'everything' for emphasis.

positions.position: Human haste and desire in the surrounding rebuke explain why the enduring deed-record must be reviewed.
positions.reasons: Ṭabāṭabāʾī says people confuse benefit and harm and pursue desires though every act remains with its doer.

positions.position: The larger section calls Jews and Quraysh to the straight path and contrasts acceptance with rejection.
positions.reasons: Iṣlāḥī says it rebukes demands for punishment by people blind to signs and alludes to God's treatment of nations.

turns_on: Which preceding theme supplies the transition to each person's record and judgment.

question: How does this verse illustrate the seven revealed modes in a reported classification?

positions.position: It exemplifies the mode concerning resurrection and accounting.
positions.reasons: Al-Burhān reports a ninth explanation of the seven modes as knowledge types: creation, unity, transcendence, attributes, commands, mercy and punishment, resurrection and accounting, and prophethood; it gives this verse as the accounting example. Al-Qāḍī says all seven noncontradictory transmitted modes entered the codex except nonmutawātir material; al-Ṭabarī and most later scholars favored one, al-Shāṭibī distinguished Abū Bakr's and ʿUthmān's compilations, and al-Ṭaḥāwī viewed the modes as temporary recitation ease.

question: What related reading and syntax issues are reported for the preceding verse?

positions.position: The doubled laqqā governs two objects, and its passive leaves one as subject and one as object.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī gives the transitivity and passive parse.

positions.position: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read the qāf with imāla, while the unchanged vowel is also acceptable.
positions.reasons: Al-Fārisī accepts both pronunciations.

turns_on: The two notes treat distinct issues in the preceding verse.

question: What ancillary rhetorical observations are included among the source notes?

positions.position: Verb-first interrogation can deny the action's occurrence or propriety.
positions.reasons: Al-Jurjānī says such a question may challenge an impossible boast or condemn a proposal; 11:28 illustrates the latter. A figurative impossible-act question compares boast or hope to absurdity rather than asserting literal expectation.

positions.position: Noun-first interrogation directs doubt to the alleged actor's identity or capacity.
positions.reasons: Al-Jurjānī distinguishes it from action-focused questioning. In 'Would he kill me while the sword is beside me?', the sword is an impediment even though the actor could kill.

positions.position: The aim of such interrogatives is to make the listener reconsider, feel shame, desist or fall silent.
positions.reasons: Al-Jurjānī treats 'denial' as a label for this effect.

positions.position: A cited Bedouin couplet and related images are praised for their figurative force.
positions.reasons: Al-Jurjānī singles out خسأت, says dawn 'permits' sight because daylight removes night's hindrance, praises the al-Jāḥiẓ couplet and Bashshār's boil image, and finds 'toil as bridge to comfort' stronger than another bridge use, also citing Rabīʿa al-Raqqī.

turns_on: The notes discuss separate rhetorical examples alongside the verse.
